etymology: Hebrew Kelach, one of the ancient cities of Asshur, a great city of the Assyrian heartland founded in the days of Nimrod.
biblical_def: Calah rises in the table of nations among the first cities of the world’s first empire. Out of the land of Shinar “went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh, and the city Rehoboth, and Calah” (Gen 10:11), “and Resen between Nineveh and Calah: the same is a great city” (Gen 10:12). Behind these foundations stands the shadow of Nimrod: “And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth” (Gen 10:8), the mighty hunter whose kingdom began at Babel. Calah was thus a jewel of the Assyrian crown, and Assyria became the rod of God’s anger against His faithless people and a byword for cruelty. Of its capital the prophet cried, “Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery” (Nah 3:1). Calah shows the double truth of the great pagan city: it is a wonder of human building and a monument of human pride, raised in the line of Nimrod who made a name against heaven. The empires of Shinar and Asshur were permitted their hour, used by God to chasten and then themselves broken. The great city that seems eternal is grass; the LORD who raised Assyria to smite Israel afterward laid Nineveh and Calah in the dust. The mighty hunter’s cities do not outlast the word of God.
webster_summary: An ancient city of Assyria founded in the line of Nimrod (Gen 10:11-12); a monument of imperial pride raised up and then broken by the God who rules the nations.

corruption_summary: An ancient Assyrian city of Nimrod’s line; the entry recovers that the proudest empire is raised for its hour and then broken by the God of the nations.
corruption_paragraphs: Calah’s abiding lesson is the vanity of empire. Founded in the line of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one and built Babel, it belonged to a civilization that made a name for itself against heaven. The great city gleamed with palaces and reliefs of conquest, and thought itself eternal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the rise and fall of nations. He raised Assyria as the rod of His anger to chasten faithless Israel, and when its pride was full He shattered it, so that Calah and Nineveh became mounds in the wilderness. Every empire that trusts its own might and forgets the LORD is grass that withers. The city of the mighty hunter is dust; the word of God stands for ever.

etymology: Hebrew Kuthah (also Cuth), a Babylonian city from which Assyria resettled colonists into Samaria after the exile of the ten tribes.
biblical_def: Cuthah gave its name to a corruption of worship. When Assyria had emptied the northern kingdom, the king “brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria” (2Ki 17:24). These transplanted peoples brought their idols with them: “the men of Cuth made Nergal” (2Ki 17:30). Terrified by lions, they added a nominal fear of the LORD to their old gods, and the result was the very definition of syncretism: “They feared the LORD, and served their own gods” (2Ki 17:33); yea, “these nations feared the LORD, and served their graven images” (2Ki 17:41). From Cuthah the later Jews named the mixed people of Samaria “Cutheans.” Here is the pattern of every false religion that will not choose between Christ and its idols. To fear the LORD and serve one’s own gods is to fear Him not at all, for He is a jealous God who will not share His glory. The men of Cuth kept Nergal on the shelf beside a borrowed reverence for Jehovah, and their worship was an abomination. No man can serve two masters; the double-minded worshipper is unstable in all his ways, and the God who demands the whole heart is not honoured by a divided one.
webster_summary: A Babylonian city whose colonists were settled in Samaria (2Ki 17:24) and mixed the fear of the LORD with the idol Nergal (2Ki 17:30-33); the very type of syncretistic worship.

corruption_summary: The Babylonian city whose colonists mingled the fear of the LORD with idols; the entry names syncretism as a false worship that honours God not at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Cuthah is the biblical archetype of syncretism. Its transplanted men added a fear of the LORD to their idol Nergal, and Scripture pronounces the verdict plainly: they feared the LORD, and served their own gods. To bolt a reverence for Jehovah onto a shelf of idols is not partial obedience but total offence, for God is jealous and will have all or nothing.

The modern form of this corruption is the widespread creed that all religions climb the same mountain, that one may honour Christ while keeping the idols of the age — self, mammon, sensuality, the approving crowd. It is Cuthah reborn: the fear of the LORD mingled with the service of graven images. But no man can serve two masters, and the double-minded worshipper is an abomination. The gospel calls not for Christ added to the idols but for the idols cast down and Christ alone enthroned. The men of Cuth kept Nergal; the true convert burns his idols in the fire.

etymology: Hebrew Chalach, a district or place in the Assyrian empire where the exiles of the northern kingdom were resettled.
biblical_def: Halah is a name of exile. When Samaria fell in Hoshea’s ninth year, the ten tribes were torn from the land of promise and scattered across the Assyrian empire: “the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes” (2Ki 17:6). The Chronicler records the same for the trans-Jordan tribes, whom God “brought unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day” (1Ch 5:26); and the historian repeats it, that Assyria “put them in Halah and in Habor” (2Ki 18:11). Halah was no random misfortune. It was the covenant curse falling exactly as Moses had foretold: “the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other” (Deu 28:64). The idolatry of Jeroboam ripened into the deportation of a nation. Halah preaches the seriousness of God’s threatenings: what He warns He performs. The tribes that would not hear the prophets heard the Assyrian trumpet, and the pleasant land was exchanged for a distant province of bondage. Yet even in Halah the covenant was not wholly spent, for a remnant according to grace was ever kept, and the God who scatters is the God who has promised to gather again.
webster_summary: A place in Assyria where the exiled ten tribes were resettled (2Ki 17:6); the covenant curse of scattering (Deu 28:64) fallen upon a people ripened in idolatry.

corruption_summary: The Assyrian place of Israel’s exile; the entry recovers the seriousness of God’s threatenings, that what He warns He surely performs.
corruption_paragraphs: Halah confronts the comfortable delusion that God’s warnings are idle words. For generations the north served the calves of Jeroboam and despised the prophets, presuming upon a patience they mistook for indifference. Then the Assyrian came, and the pleasant land was exchanged for the distant province of Halah, exactly as Moses had foretold.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the threatenings of God are as sure as His promises. The age loves a God who never judges, whose love could not permit any lasting punishment; but Halah stands in the record as proof that the curse of the covenant falls when sin is ripe. He who scattered Israel from one end of the earth to the other is not mocked. Yet the same God kept a remnant according to grace, and He who scatters has promised in Christ to gather His own from every land.

etymology: Hebrew Chelbon, “fruitful” or “fat,” a place near Damascus famed for its wine, named in the lament over Tyre.
biblical_def: Helbon appears once, as a luxury on the manifest of a doomed merchant-city. In Ezekiel’s great lamentation over Tyre, the prophet catalogues the riches that flowed into her markets: “Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool” (Eze 27:18). The wine of Helbon was a byword for the finest vintage, poured, ancient records say, at the tables of kings. It came to Tyre, that queen of commerce for whom the prophet was bidden, “take up a lamentation for Tyrus” (Eze 27:2). Tyre had enriched the earth: “thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise” (Eze 27:33). Yet all her wealth, the wine of Helbon and the white wool and the treasures of the seas, could not save her from the judgment of God. Helbon thus stands as a small emblem of luxury under sentence. The wine is good in itself, a gift of God to gladden the heart of man; but the heart that makes riches and pleasure its trust is warned: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red” (Pro 23:31). The finest vintage cannot ransom a soul, and the proudest market falls when its cup of iniquity is full.
webster_summary: A place near Damascus famed for its wine, named in the lament over Tyre (Eze 27:18); an emblem of the luxury that cannot ransom a city under the judgment of God.

corruption_paragraphs: Helbon’s single mention names a luxury — the finest wine — flowing into the market of doomed Tyre. The wine itself is a good gift of God, given to gladden the heart of man; the corruption is not in the vintage but in the trust. Tyre made her riches her god and reckoned herself untouchable.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that abundance is a stewardship, not a security. The consumer age, like Tyre, heaps to itself the wine of Helbon and the wares of the world and imagines that comfort is salvation. But the finest cup cannot ransom a soul, and the wealthiest city falls when its iniquity is full. Let the Christian receive God’s good gifts with thanksgiving and sobriety, remembering that the treasure which endures is laid up in heaven, not poured in the goblets of Tyre.

etymology: Hebrew Shin'ar, the ancient name of the plain of Babylonia, the cradle of Babel and the earliest kingdoms of the earth.
biblical_def: Shinar is the land where man first built his rebellion into a city. There the sons of men gathered after the flood: “as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there” (Gen 11:2), and there they raised the tower of Babel to make themselves a name. Shinar was the seedbed of empire: “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar” (Gen 10:10). From Shinar came Amraphel, one of the kings who warred against Sodom: “in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar” (Gen 14:1). And to Shinar, in Zechariah’s vision, wickedness itself is carried and given a house: “To build it an house in the land of Shinar: and it shall be established, and set there upon her own base” (Zec 5:11). So Shinar becomes in Scripture the very geography of man’s godless unity — the plain where humanity, one in tongue and purpose, set itself against heaven. It is the type of Babylon in every age: the confederacy of the proud, the city that would climb to God by its own bricks and mortar. Against Babel the LORD came down and scattered the tongues; against every Shinar since, He sets His face. The one true unity of mankind is not the tower of the plain but the body of Christ, gathered by the Spirit from every scattered tongue.
webster_summary: The plain of Babylonia, cradle of Babel and the first kingdoms (Gen 10:10; 11:2); the biblical type of man’s godless unity set against heaven.

corruption_summary: The plain of Babel and the first empires; the entry recovers Shinar as the type of man’s godless unity, answered only by the gathering of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Shinar is the birthplace of the enduring corruption of Babel: mankind united in tongue and purpose to build a name against heaven. The tower of the plain is the perpetual dream of a humanity that would ascend to God, or dethrone Him, by its own brick and slime. Every empire of the proud is a new Shinar.

The modern tower is the utopian project of a borderless, godless oneness — a single human city, managed by man, needing no heaven. It is Babel in glass and steel, and it ends as Babel ended, in confusion and scattering, for the LORD resists the proud. The true and lasting unity of the human race is not the confederacy of Shinar but the church, one body gathered by the Spirit out of every scattered tongue (Rev 5:9). Pentecost answers Babel: what pride divided, grace unites, under one Lord and not one tower.

etymology: Hebrew Ellasar, a city-kingdom of Mesopotamia whose king Arioch joined the eastern coalition against the cities of the plain.
biblical_def: Ellasar is known only as the seat of a king in Abraham’s day. When four eastern kings marched to subdue the rebellious cities of the plain, Arioch of Ellasar rode among them: “in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations” (Gen 14:1). Again the record names him in the battle: “with Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Gen 14:9). These were the great powers of the age, and they swept Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot with the spoil. Then a stranger thing happened than any conquest. Abraham, with three hundred and eighteen trained servants, overtook the victorious kings, and “brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot” (Gen 14:16). Melchizedek met him with bread and wine and blessed “the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand” (Gen 14:20). Ellasar and its allies preach that the mightiest confederacy of kings is nothing before the God of Abraham. The powers of Mesopotamia mustered their chariots; one man of faith, armed with the promise, put them to flight. The battle is the LORD’s, and He delights to overturn the great by the weak that trust in Him.
webster_summary: A Mesopotamian city-kingdom whose king Arioch joined the eastern coalition against Sodom (Gen 14:1,9); routed, with its allies, by Abraham and the God who delivers enemies into the hand of faith.

corruption_summary: The Mesopotamian kingdom of Arioch in the eastern coalition; the entry recovers that the mightiest league of kings is nothing before the God of Abraham.
corruption_paragraphs: Ellasar figures in the first war recorded in Scripture, a coalition of great eastern powers that seemed irresistible. The lesson is not in the kingdom’s obscurity but in its defeat: the confederacy that plundered the cities of the plain was overturned by a single man of faith with three hundred and eighteen servants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD delivers the enemies of His people into the hand of faith. The world reckons by the number of kings and the count of chariots; Abraham reckoned by the promise of God. Melchizedek blessed the most high God who had given the victory, and Abraham gave tithes of all. Ellasar and its allies stand as the first proof in Scripture that the battle is the LORD’s, and that He is pleased to scatter the mighty by the weak who trust in Him.

etymology: Hebrew Merathayim, “double rebellion” or “double bitterness,” a symbolic name for Babylon in Jeremiah’s oracle of judgment.
biblical_def: Merathaim is not so much a place as a verdict. In Jeremiah’s great prophecy against Babylon, the LORD summons the destroyer against the land under a name that spells out its guilt: “Go up against the land of Merathaim, even against it, and against the inhabitants of Pekod: waste and utterly destroy after them, saith the LORD” (Jer 50:21). The name means “double rebellion,” and it fastens upon Babylon the twofold charge of pride against God and cruelty against His people. The whole oracle is set against the golden city: “The word that the LORD spake against Babylon and against the land of the Chaldeans by Jeremiah the prophet” (Jer 50:1). His people are called out of her before the blow falls: “Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and deliver every man his soul” (Jer 51:6). And the New Testament takes up the same cry over the final Babylon: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen” (Rev 18:2). Merathaim teaches that God names sin truly and judges it exactly. The empire that flattered itself as eternal was, in heaven’s ledger, simply Double-Rebellion, ripe for the sword. Every proud power that rebels against God and oppresses His church wears the same name in His sight, and the same doom awaits it. The LORD does the naming, and His naming is the sentence.
webster_summary: A symbolic name for Babylon meaning “double rebellion” (Jer 50:21); heaven’s true verdict upon the proud empire ripe for judgment.

corruption_summary: The symbolic name for Babylon, “double rebellion”; the entry recovers that God names sin truly and judges the proud empire exactly.
corruption_paragraphs: Merathaim strips the disguise from Babylon. The city called herself the golden queen of kingdoms; heaven called her Double-Rebellion. The name is the corruption named: pride against God and bitterness against His people, doubled and full. God does not flatter the powerful; He weighs them and writes their true name in His book.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the truthful judgment of God, who calls sin by its right name however the world gilds it. Empires and idols and ideologies present themselves in glittering titles; the LORD sees Merathaim, double rebellion, and appoints the sword. His people are commanded to come out of Babylon and not share her iniquity or her plagues. The final Babylon falls as the first did, and the same voice that named Merathaim cries, Babylon the great is fallen. God’s naming is His sentence, and His sentence is sure.

etymology: Hebrew Peqod, “visitation” or “punishment,” the name of an Aramean people east of the Tigris, used in prophecy as a byword for the region of Babylon under judgment.
biblical_def: Pekod names a people and a punishment at once. The Pekod were an Aramean tribe of the lower Tigris, reckoned among the might of Babylon: Ezekiel lists them among the LORD’s instruments of chastening against faithless Jerusalem — “The Babylonians, and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, and Shoa, and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them” (Eze 23:23). These were the lovers Judah had courted and who would turn to devour her: “I will raise up thy lovers against thee, from whom thy mind is alienated” (Eze 23:22). Yet the very name Pekod means visitation, and Jeremiah turns it back upon Babylon itself in a stroke of holy irony: “against the inhabitants of Pekod: waste and utterly destroy after them, saith the LORD” (Jer 50:21). The rod that God used to punish Judah would itself be visited: “Behold, I am against thee, O thou most proud, saith the Lord GOD of hosts: for thy day is come, the time that I will visit thee” (Jer 50:31). Pekod teaches the double edge of God’s justice. He raises up the wicked to chasten His people, then punishes the wicked for the very cruelty He overruled. The Assyrian and the Babylonian were His axe and His saw, yet the axe does not boast against the hand that swings it (Isa 10:15). The instrument of visitation is itself visited; none escapes the reckoning of God.
webster_summary: An Aramean people of the Tigris, an instrument of Babylon’s might (Eze 23:23) whose name “visitation” Jeremiah turns back as Babylon’s own doom (Jer 50:21).

corruption_summary: The Aramean people whose name means “visitation”; the entry recovers that God’s instruments of wrath are themselves visited for their sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Pekod illustrates a hard and holy truth: that God uses the wicked to chasten His people and then judges the wicked for their wickedness. The Babylonians and their allied tribes were the rod in His hand against Jerusalem’s harlotry, yet they were not thereby innocent. The name that means visitation was fitted first to Judah’s punishment and then to Babylon’s.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty and the justice of God together. He is not the author of the cruelty He overrules, and the axe does not boast against Him that heweth with it (Isa 10:15). The proud instrument of His anger is itself brought to the day of visitation. This forbids both the despair that thinks the wicked triumph unchecked and the pride that imagines itself God’s favourite because it prospers as His rod. All flesh is weighed; none escapes the reckoning; the LORD visits every Pekod in its hour.

etymology: Hebrew Ahava, a river and the place beside it in Babylonia where Ezra gathered the returning exiles to fast and pray before the journey to Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Ahava is a place of prayer on the eve of a hard road. When Ezra led the second company of exiles home, he mustered them by this river: “And I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days” (Ezr 8:15). Finding no Levites among them, he sent for ministers, and then, before setting out across a bandit-ridden wilderness with the treasure of the temple and their little ones, he did not ask the king for soldiers. He called a fast: “Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance” (Ezr 8:21). He was ashamed to request a guard, having testified that God’s hand was upon them for good. “So we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was intreated of us” (Ezr 8:23). And the LORD answered: “the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy” (Ezr 8:31). Ahava preaches the sufficiency of prayer and the honour of a faith that dares to trust God rather than the arm of flesh. Ezra stood upon his confession and sought the Lord, and the way was made safe. The river of Ahava is a monument to answered prayer and to the God who is entreated of them that seek Him.

corruption_summary: The river where Ezra fasted before the return; the entry recovers the sufficiency of prayer and the honour of trusting God above the arm of flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahava faces no modern quarrel, but it rebukes the reflex that reaches first for the arm of flesh. Ezra had a perilous road, a caravan of treasure, and helpless little ones; the natural course was to beg the king for a band of soldiers. Instead he was ashamed to contradict his own testimony that God’s hand was upon them, and he called a fast.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prayer and fasting are real means by which God is genuinely entreated. Our age trusts the guard, the insurance, the contingency, and treats prayer as a sentiment rather than a power. Ezra staked the lives of women and children on the faithfulness of God, sought Him with fasting, and was heard: the hand of our God was upon us. Ahava calls the church to afflict itself before God in earnest supplication, and to believe that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him.

etymology: Aramaic Achmetha, the city of Ecbatana, capital of Media, where the decree of Cyrus concerning the temple was found in the royal archives.
biblical_def: Achmetha, the Ecbatana of the Medes, is the place where a lost decree was found and a great work saved. When the enemies of the returned exiles challenged their right to rebuild the temple, Darius ordered a search of the records, “and there was found at Achmetha, in the palace that is in the province of the Medes, a roll, and therein was a record thus written” (Ezr 6:2). The search had begun in Babylon — “search was made in the house of the rolls, where the treasures were laid up in Babylon” (Ezr 6:1) — but it was in the summer palace of Achmetha that the decree of Cyrus lay preserved: “In the first year of Cyrus the king the same Cyrus the king made a decree concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, Let the house be builded” (Ezr 6:3). On the strength of that recovered scroll, Darius confirmed the work and commanded its costs to be paid from the royal treasury. Achmetha is a quiet monument to the providence that governs archives and kings. A pagan decree, filed years before and forgotten by men, was kept by God in a Median palace against the very day His people needed it. “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). The temple rose because God had hidden a scroll in Achmetha.
webster_summary: Ecbatana, the Median capital where the lost decree of Cyrus was found (Ezr 6:2); a monument to the providence that guards archives and turns the hearts of kings.

corruption_summary: Ecbatana, where the lost decree of Cyrus was found; the entry recovers the providence that guards archives and turns the hearts of kings for His church.
corruption_paragraphs: Achmetha raises no modern controversy, yet the finding of the scroll rebukes the notion that the work of God hangs upon human vigilance alone. A decree filed and forgotten in a Median palace was the hinge on which the whole rebuilding turned. Men had lost it; God had kept it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the meticulous providence of God over the smallest instruments of His purpose — a filed roll, a king’s memory, a clerk’s search. He turns the heart of Darius as He turned the heart of Cyrus, for the king’s heart is in His hand as the rivers of water (Pro 21:1). The church builds under the eye of a God who prepared her provisions before she knew her need, hiding a scroll in Achmetha against the day of Darius. What men mislay, God preserves; what enemies would forbid, He commands to be paid from their own treasury.
